content:
According to reports yesterday, Apple has agreed to comply with the EU's "more fair" App Tracking Transparency (ATT) rules, following an investigation by the German antitrust authority.

Apple stated that it is voluntarily complying with the regulations. We understand it will make a total of eight changes to achieve compliance...

Developers often collect far more personal data than is necessary for app functionality. What Apple refers to as "app tracking" is one example: using the interests displayed by the apps you have installed to serve you personalised ads, whether within apps or on the web. App Tracking Transparency (ATT) lets you choose whether this data can be collected and used in this way.

Apple said yesterday that Germany's Federal Cartel Office (FCO) recognises the value of giving users a choice; in fact, the FCO's report noted that it welcomes the introduction of ATT from a data protection perspective, and other privacy regulators within Germany hold the same position.

The FCO's objection appears to be that Apple's current prompt wording makes app tracking sound scarier than it actually is. The iPhone maker will make eight changes to address this — including removing the word "track".

  • Change the colour of the icon element above the prompt from orange to blue
  • Update the ATT prompt to display in full screen
  • Remove the word "track" from the ATT prompt and the personalised ads prompt
  • Change the ATT prompt's selection buttons from "Allow" and "Ask App Not to Track" to "Allow" and "Reject"
  • Allow formatting (such as bold, italics and bulleted lists) to be used within the ATT prompt
  • Add an option for developers to display an additional page of information directly from the prompt, providing further GDPR-related information. Developers can actually already achieve this using prompts shown before the ATT prompt.
  • Allow developers to display the ATT prompt to users again one year after they make a decision, whether their choice was "consent" or "reject"
  • Make minor wording adjustments to the personalised ads prompt to improve clarity, but the effect or meaning of the wording remains unchanged

Apple told us that it is committed to ensuring ATT continues to be available in EU countries, and the measure has been welcomed by privacy advocates, data protection authorities and iPhone users.

The company reiterated that the reason its own apps do not show the ATT prompt is because it does not use personal data collected from apps to deliver targeted advertising or measure advertising effectiveness. It stressed that third-party apps are treated exactly the same way — if a third-party app does not collect such data, there is no need to show the prompt.

9to5Mac Review

For all parties, this appears to be the ideal outcome. iPhone users will continue to make a choice, but based on a prompt that more accurately reflects the decision they need to make — that is, the trade-off between personalised ads and no personalised ads.

This investigation also addressed external concerns about Apple's own advertising sales business. The company has clearly stated that it does not use data collected by its apps to deliver personalised ads, nor does it use such data to measure advertising effectiveness.
